activities.title: Grounding 5–4–3–2–1
activities.description: A short exercise for the senses that brings your attention to what you can see, feel and hear right now.
activities.purpose: Helps bring your attention back to the present moment when nervousness or anxiety carries you away.
steps: Sit or stand steadily and breathe calmly.
In your mind, name five things you can see.
Name four things you can feel by touch – for example the back of the chair or the floor under your feet.
Name three sounds you can hear.
Name two smells and one taste – or two things you like.
Finally, notice how you feel now. Nothing needs to change.
activities.caution: If the exercise brings up strong memories or increases your anxiety, stop and go back to what you were doing. The exercise does not replace help in a crisis.

activities.title: Calm breathing 4–6
activities.description: A breathing exercise in which the out-breath is a little longer than the in-breath.
activities.purpose: A slow out-breath can calm the body in a tense situation, for example before a meeting or when going to bed.
steps: Settle into a comfortable position and let your shoulders drop.
Breathe in calmly through your nose, counting to about four.
Breathe out slowly, counting to about six.
Repeat for about three minutes at your own pace.
Finally, go back to normal breathing and notice how your body feels.
activities.caution: If you start to feel dizzy or breathing feels uncomfortable, go back to normal breathing. If you have a respiratory condition, do the exercise gently or skip it.

activities.title: Worry time
activities.description: You write your worries down and set aside a separate, limited time for them during the day.
activities.purpose: When worries go round in your mind all day or in the evening, moving them to an agreed time can make you feel lighter.
steps: Set aside 15 minutes of worry time in your day, for example in the early evening – not just before bed.
When a worry comes to mind at other times, write it down briefly.
Go back to what you were doing and remind yourself that the worry has its own time.
During worry time, go through the list: what can you influence, and what can you not?
When the time is up, stop – you can continue tomorrow.
activities.caution: If your worries are about your own or someone else's safety, don't postpone them – get help straight away.

activities.title: One small next step
activities.description: From the things going round in your mind, you choose one small step you can actually take.
activities.purpose: When things seem to pile up, choosing one small step can make the situation more manageable.
steps: Write down the things that are going round in your mind.
Choose one of them that is small and doable today or tomorrow.
Break it down into the first concrete step, for example “I’ll open the message and read it”.
Decide when you will take the step.
Once you have taken the step, notice it – even if it feels small.
activities.caution: Choose something really small. The aim is not to get more done but to make things feel lighter.
activities.sourcePlaceholder: Source: [placeholder] – a self-care programme approved by a professional.

activities.title: Looking at your evening routine
activities.description: A short look at your routines on recent evenings, and one small experiment.
activities.purpose: Looking at your evening routines can help you notice small things that support rest.
steps: Think back to recent evenings: what did you do in the hour before going to bed?
Notice what seemed to calm you down and what seemed to wake you up.
Choose one small thing to try on a few evenings – for example screens off half an hour earlier.
In the morning, write down briefly how the night felt.
activities.caution: This exercise does not replace treatment for sleep problems. If your sleep problems are long-lasting or severe, tell a professional about them.

activities.title: Your support network
activities.description: You identify the people and services you can contact.
activities.purpose: Knowing who you can turn to can ease the feeling of being alone.
steps: Think of the people you feel at least a little safe with.
Choose one of them and think of a small way to be in touch: a message, a call or a meeting.
If you like, you can send a short message today.
Also write down one service you can contact if you need help.
activities.caution: If nobody comes to mind right now, that is understandable. You can also write down a professional or a service.

activities.title: Values and one value-based action
activities.description: Identifying your own values and taking one small action in line with them.
activities.purpose: Identifying your own values can give you a sense of direction, even when things feel heavy.
steps: Think about what matters to you in life – for example the people close to you, health, learning or nature.
Choose one value that feels meaningful right now.
Think of one small action in line with this value.
Do it this week and notice how it felt – without judging.
activities.caution: The aim is not to be perfect. Even a small action is enough.
activities.sourcePlaceholder: Source: [placeholder] – a self-care programme approved by a professional.

activities.title: Planning something pleasant
activities.description: You plan ahead one small pleasant or meaningful thing for this week.
activities.purpose: When your energy is low, planning a small pleasant thing in advance can make it easier to actually do it.
steps: Think about what has brought you even a little joy, calm or meaning before.
Choose a small version of it for this week, for example a 10-minute walk.
Decide on a day and a time and write it in your calendar.
Afterwards, notice how it felt – without judging.
activities.caution: Choose something realistic for the energy you have now. If it doesn't work out, it is not a failure – you can try something smaller.
